name: Snake Plant

images.label: Snake plant in white ceramic pot with decorative pebbles, near entrance

watering.notes: Extremely drought-tolerant. Let soil dry out completely between waterings — root rot from overwatering is the #1 killer of this plant, far more likely than underwatering.

fertilizing.fertilizerType: Balanced diluted liquid fertilizer (e.g. 10-10-10 at half strength)
fertilizing.notes: Only feed during active growth (spring/summer); skip entirely in winter.

pruning.notes: Remove any yellowing or damaged leaves at the base.

environment.light: Tolerates low light but grows best in bright, indirect light
environment.pruningStyle: Cut damaged leaves at the soil line with a clean blade
environment.notes: Toughest plant on this list — near-impossible to kill through neglect, easy to kill through overwatering.

notes: One long leaf appears to be trailing a thin wire/string in the photo — worth checking it isn't constricting new growth.

images.label: Thryallis with yellow flower spikes, terracotta rectangular planter, street view behind
Chrysanthemum bush in foreground with Thryallis pot visible alongside
Thryallis flower spikes, confirmed as sharing its planter with Ixora, not the same plant
Thryallis and Ixora planter, with chrysanthemum bush in the adjacent pot

watering.notes: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged, especially in a shallow planter that dries fast in balcony sun. During Bangalore's August monsoon, natural rainfall likely reduces how often you need to top this up — check soil moisture before watering rather than sticking rigidly to a 3-day count.

fertilizing.notes: Regular feeding keeps the yellow flower spikes coming; it's a fairly heavy bloomer.

pruning.notes: Light shaping after flush of blooms fades encourages denser re-flowering.

environment.light: Full sun to part sun for best flowering
environment.pruningStyle: Trim leggy stems by a third after a bloom cycle
environment.notes: Fast-growing and fairly forgiving; good balcony plant for continuous color.

name: Peperomia (Raindrop)
location: Balcony floor, near lantern and other potted plants

images.label: Peperomia in dark plastic pot, balcony corner with morning light

watering.notes: Semi-succulent leaves store water — let the top 2-3 inches of soil dry before watering again.

fertilizing.notes: Light feeder; over-fertilizing causes leggy growth.

pruning.notes: Pinch leggy stems to keep it bushy.

environment.light: Bright, indirect light; some morning sun is fine

name: Dahlia (White)
location: Balcony railing planter, shared with Chrysanthemum

images.label: White dahlia blooms and magenta chrysanthemum sharing a terracotta planter

watering.notes: Keep evenly moist; dahlias are thirsty bloomers and wilt quickly if the pot dries out in sun.

fertilizing.notes: Too much nitrogen gives leafy growth at the cost of flowers.

pruning.notes: Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep new buds forming.

environment.pruningStyle: Snip spent flower heads just above a leaf pair
environment.notes: Sharing a planter with a chrysanthemum means both compete for water/nutrients — worth watching if one starts outcompeting the other.

name: Chrysanthemum (Magenta)

images.label: Magenta chrysanthemum blooms sharing planter with white dahlia
Close-up of magenta chrysanthemum blooms
Chrysanthemum bush, mostly foliage with buds not yet open
Same feathery-leaved, not-yet-blooming chrysanthemum bush, next to the Thryallis/Ixora planter
Not-yet-blooming chrysanthemum bush, with an orange Kalanchoe pot visible beside it
Fully bloomed magenta and dark-purple chrysanthemum, sharing a planter with white dahlia

watering.notes: Likes consistently moist soil; wilts fast when dry, recovers well once watered. Outdoor pots will need less top-up watering during Bangalore's August rains — check soil before adding water.

fertilizing.fertilizerType: Balanced liquid feed, switching to bloom booster once buds form

pruning.notes: Deadhead spent flowers; pinch growing tips early in the season for bushier plants and more blooms.

environment.notes: You weren't sure if these are the same plant, and the new photos actually point toward two separate pots rather than one: the leafy, not-yet-blooming bush consistently appears next to the Thryallis/Ixora planter and separately next to the orange Kalanchoe pot, while the fully bloomed magenta/purple chrysanthemum appears in its own planter alongside the white dahlia. Treating this as two chrysanthemum pots (one still budding, one in full bloom) is the safer read — worth a quick visual confirmation next time you're on the balcony.

notes: Likely two separate pots of chrysanthemums rather than one plant at different times — see environment notes.

images.label: Young seedlings/cuttings propagating in a grey textured pot

watering.notes: Seedlings have shallow roots and dry out fast — keep soil lightly moist, never soggy.

fertilizing.fertilizerType: Diluted balanced liquid fertilizer, only once true leaves are established
fertilizing.notes: Hold off feeding until seedlings are a few weeks old.

repotting.potSize: Currently a shared starter pot — will need separating soon

pruning.notes: Pinch tops once seedlings reach 4-6 leaves to encourage branching.

environment.light: Bright light, several hours of direct sun once established
environment.notes: These look crowded in one pot — thinning/transplanting individual seedlings will help each one thrive.

images.label: Full, healthy areca palm in ribbed white ceramic pot next to sofa and guitar

watering.notes: Water when the top inch of soil is dry. Sensitive to fluoride/chlorine and salt buildup — tips brown if water quality or overwatering is an issue; filtered/rain water is ideal.

repotting.soilType: Well-draining potting mix with peat/coco coir

pruning.notes: Trim fully brown fronds at the base; leave partially yellow ones until fully brown.

environment.light: Bright, indirect light; avoid direct harsh sun
environment.humidity: Prefers higher humidity — mist occasionally or use a pebble tray indoors
environment.pruningStyle: Cut spent fronds at the base with clean shears
environment.notes: Looks like the healthiest plant in the collection — good indoor light and consistent care.

name: Kalanchoe (Orange)
location: Balcony railing planter, shared with Rose

images.label: Orange kalanchoe blooms sharing planter with red rose
Kalanchoe and rose, wider angle showing shared planter
Close-up of orange kalanchoe clusters sharing the planter with red and dark-red roses

watering.notes: Succulent-type — let soil dry between waterings. Being in a planter shared with a thirstier rose means watch for overwatering here specifically.

repotting.soilType: Well-draining mix; ideally a sandier mix than what the rose needs

pruning.notes: Deadhead spent flower clusters to prolong blooming.

environment.light: Bright light, several hours of direct sun for reblooming
environment.notes: Kalanchoe wants drier soil than roses — sharing a pot is workable but not ideal long-term; consider separating if either starts struggling.

name: Rose (Red)
location: Balcony railing planter, shared with Kalanchoe

images.label: Red rose bloom sharing planter with orange kalanchoe
Two red rose blooms with orange kalanchoe alongside
Close-up showing at least 3-4 rose blooms including a darker maroon variety, plus kalanchoe alongside

watering.notes: Roses want consistently moist (not soggy) soil, deep watering rather than frequent shallow sips. Bangalore's August rains should reduce the need for manual top-ups outdoors — check soil moisture rather than watering on autopilot, since roses also dislike sitting in waterlogged soil during heavy rain spells.

fertilizing.notes: Feed during active growth/blooming season, hold back in dormancy.

repotting.potSize: Shared rectangular planter — on the small side for a rose long-term
repotting.soilType: Rich loamy mix with good drainage

pruning.notes: Deadhead spent blooms just above a 5-leaflet leaf; harder structural prune once a year in the dormant season.

environment.humidity: Average; good airflow helps prevent fungal issues
environment.pruningStyle: Angled cut above an outward-facing bud
environment.notes: Watch for blackspot/powdery mildew given balcony humidity; the shared planter with kalanchoe may run drier than roses prefer.

notes: The close-up shows what look like two rose color variants in this planter — bright red and a darker maroon/burgundy. Could be two different rose plants rather than one, worth a glance next time you're watering.

name: Ixora (Jungle Flame)
location: Balcony railing planter, interplanted with Thryallis

images.label: Ixora with glossy leaves and red buds, Thryallis flowering alongside
Close-up confirming red buds and glossy oval leaves typical of Ixora coccinea
Wider shot confirming Ixora and Thryallis as two distinct plants sharing one planter, chrysanthemum bush nearby

watering.notes: Likes consistently moist soil, doesn't tolerate drying out well — buds can drop if it goes too dry between waterings. In Bangalore's August monsoon, outdoor rainfall may cover most of this on its own; check soil before adding more water rather than watering on a fixed schedule.

fertilizing.fertilizerType: Acidic-leaning fertilizer (Ixora prefers slightly acidic soil, similar to hibiscus feed)
fertilizing.notes: Yellowing between leaf veins on Ixora is often an iron/micronutrient deficiency from soil pH being too alkaline — worth watching for.

repotting.potSize: Shared rectangular terracotta planter with Thryallis

pruning.notes: Deadhead spent flower clusters; light shaping keeps it compact and blooming.

environment.light: Full sun to bright part sun for best flowering
environment.humidity: Likes humidity — Bangalore's monsoon-season air should suit it well
environment.pruningStyle: Snip spent flower clusters just above a leaf node
environment.notes: Confirmed as Ixora coccinea from the close-up — glossy leaves and clustered red buds are a clear match.

notes: Grows in the same planter as the Thryallis but is a separate plant, per your confirmation.

name: Syngonium Living Wall
species: Syngonium podophyllum (pink and green cultivars, arrowhead vine)

images.label: Vertical living wall of syngonium, mixed pink and green varieties, many leaves dried/browning
Close-up of dried, hanging syngonium leaves at top of the living wall

watering.notes: URGENT: this wall looks significantly under-watered/stressed — large portions are dried and crispy. Vertical planters drain and dry fast, especially upper rows. Consider checking the irrigation drippers are actually reaching every cell, not just watering frequency.

fertilizing.notes: Hold off feeding stressed sections until they recover — fertilizing dry, damaged roots can do more harm than good.

repotting.potSize: Individual cells in modular vertical planter system
repotting.soilType: Light, moisture-retentive mix (coco coir blend works well in vertical systems)

pruning.notes: Cut away fully dead/brown growth now to redirect energy to the still-green sections, and to assess how much of the wall is actually salvageable.

environment.light: Bright, indirect light; the pink cultivars in particular need decent light to hold color without scorching
environment.humidity: Prefers higher humidity — vertical outdoor walls can dry out fast in wind/sun
environment.pruningStyle: Cut dead vines back to green, healthy stem
environment.notes: This is the one plant grouping on the list that needs real intervention, not just routine care — the ratio of brown/dried to green in the photos suggests either an irrigation failure or a prolonged dry spell.

notes: Flagging this as the priority: worth checking the irrigation system on this wall specifically before anything else on the list.

name: Purple Heart (Tradescantia)
species: Tradescantia pallida (or T. zebrina — leaf shape suggests pallida)
location: Near the living wall structure, on the floor

images.label: Purple/violet tradescantia in white pot, dried living wall visible behind

watering.notes: Fairly drought-tolerant once established; let soil dry somewhat between waterings, but don't neglect for too long or lower leaves shrivel.

pruning.notes: Pinch/trim leggy trailing stems to keep it full; trimmings root easily in water if you want more plants.

environment.light: Bright light to some direct sun — purple color intensifies with more light, fades to green in low light

name: Philodendron (Large-leaf)
species: Philodendron sp. (large arrow-shaped leaves — possibly P. giganteum or similar large-leaf hybrid)

images.label: Wider indoor hallway shot, near kitchen entrance
Close-up clearly showing marginal leaf browning, one fully yellowed leaf with brown spotting, and a curling/drooping habit

watering.notes: Water when the top inch or two of soil is dry. You weren't sure of the recent watering pattern, so treat this as a starting point rather than a fix — the close-up shows classic marginal browning (crispy edges working inward) plus one leaf that's gone fully yellow with brown spotting, which most often points to a stretch of underwatering or a dry indoor environment rather than overwatering (overwatered leaves usually go soft and mushy, not crispy at the margins).

fertilizing.notes: Hold off feeding until you've settled on a consistent watering rhythm — feeding a plant that's dealing with a watering/humidity issue won't fix the underlying cause and can add salt stress on top of it.

repotting.potSize: Medium ribbed ceramic pot with saucer
repotting.soilType: Chunky aroid mix (bark, perlite, peat/coco coir)

pruning.notes: Remove the fully brown/crisped leaf visible in the photo — it won't recover and is drawing energy away from healthy growth.

environment.humidity: Prefers moderate-high humidity; indoor hallway air can be drier than this plant likes
environment.pruningStyle: Cut fully damaged leaves at the base of the petiole
environment.notes: The leaf browning pattern (edges in first, following the leaf margin, one leaf gone fully yellow with brown blotching) leans toward underwatering and/or low ambient humidity for this genus — the close-up rules out the mushy/translucent look typical of overwatering.

notes: Since the recent care history is unknown, the most useful next step is simply establishing a consistent watering check (finger-test the soil every few days) rather than guessing further from photos. The damaged leaves themselves won't recover — safe to trim them once you're confident the cause is addressed, so the plant isn't spending energy on tissue that's already gone.
